regime.name: Allocation Economy
regime.definition: A market regime in which structurally insufficient supply is distributed increasingly through allocation, prioritization, forecast quality, strategic relevance and confirmed production capacity rather than normal order intake alone.
regime.distinctionFromPandemic: Unlike the pandemic supply-chain shock, the physical production and logistics network is broadly functioning. The present constraint is driven primarily by demand exceeding prioritized semiconductor and finished-goods capacity, with secondary effects spreading into lead-time visibility, logistics, cargo insurance and proof requirements.
regime.effectiveAvailableSupply: Nominal inventory is not equivalent to commercially usable inventory. Effective Available Supply is the subset that meets customer-specific eligibility requirements such as country of origin, manufacturer process/bucket code, packaging integrity, OEM qualification and verifiable provenance.
regime.proofOfInventory: In the Allocation Economy, physical inventory is increasingly accepted as commercially available only when visual evidence can verify the relevant attributes and chain of custody. Proof may be required by multiple downstream levels of the channel.
observedTransmission: Demand exceeds available or prioritized capacity
Allocation replaces normal selling for constrained products
Nominal inventory is reduced to Effective Available Supply by COO, process-code, packaging-integrity and OEM-eligibility filters
Proof-of-Inventory and visual chain-of-custody evidence become part of the commercial transaction
Lead-time visibility deteriorates before a firm delivery date can be quoted
High component prices raise shipment values
Cargo insurance and carrier value limits force physically unnecessary shipment splitting
Additional handling and transport complexity becomes a secondary availability constraint

indicators.note: The 28 August channel review confirms that Server-RDIMMs remain scarce and confirmed shipment quantities remain restricted. Micron's broad 15–20% price increase provides no evidence of physical supply relief.
UDIMM availability is broadly adequate; 32 GB UDIMMs are materially cheaper than comparable 32 GB ECC registered modules.

The 28 August channel review confirms that Enterprise SSD availability remains constrained; absent inventory, quoted lead times remain typically 6–10 weeks. Micron's selective price increase provides no evidence of broad supply relief, while the unchanged 60 TB class is tracked as a product-specific pricing exception.
Enterprise SSD supplier pricing is currently being increased on a recurring 4–6 week cadence; no uniform percentage magnitude is asserted.

Stripe's investor communication identifies 1 January 2026 as the start of a material AI-driven economic phase change, alongside strong H1 growth and rapidly scaling AI-native activity. Stripe's OpenRouter acquisition adds another observation point into model and agent usage. MT·AI treats this as leading evidence for AI-demand acceleration, not as proof of AGI or a technological singularity.

Financial Times reporting, corroborated by Reuters, says ByteDance and Tencent have each received about 10,000 Nvidia H200 processors in mainland China. US approvals may permit purchases up to 100,000 H200s per company, while Chinese NDRC reviews and Beijing's preference for deployment outside mainland China keep the channel constrained. MT·AI treats the deliveries as material evidence that previously theoretical China high-end AI compute demand is converting into physical deployments.

The H200 channel into China is opening but remains governed by dual US licensing/testing constraints and Chinese NDRC approvals. Beijing is simultaneously promoting domestic accelerators and steering some Nvidia deployments toward Hong Kong. MT·AI interprets this as evidence of a segmented China AI compute stack: Nvidia remains important for demanding training while domestic accelerators increasingly absorb inference workloads.

TrendForce/DRAMeXchange reports that steady AI-server demand, particularly for enterprise SSDs, drove a NAND supply shortage in 2Q26 and enabled significant contract ASP increases. Combined NAND revenue of the top five public brands rose 77% QoQ to US$68.87 billion. Micron NAND revenue reached US$11.85 billion, up 99.2% QoQ, moving Micron to third place. MT·AI treats this as strong confirmation that AI/eSSD demand is materially tightening the NAND market despite weak smartphone and PC demand.

TrendForce says NAND suppliers achieved significant ASP increases in 2Q26 and expects ASPs to continue supporting industry revenue growth in 3Q26. Suppliers are prioritizing DRAM and HBM capex, limiting incremental NAND capacity. The signal captures the structural chain AI/eSSD demand -> NAND shortage -> higher ASPs while DRAM/HBM investment priorities constrain supply relief.

A current large-volume request for approximately 1,300 enterprise SSDs has remained without NAND allocation approval for two weeks. NAND release may not occur until September, and finished SSD production can begin only after allocation. No reliable finished-drive delivery date can currently be quoted. MT·AI distinguishes lead-time visibility from lead-time length: an unconfirmed production start is a stronger allocation signal than a long but firm delivery date.

A separate 60 TB enterprise SSD project shows that NAND availability and allocation do not equal finished-drive availability: NAND was available and allocated, yet finished SSD delivery exceeds two months. MT·AI therefore tracks upstream NAND allocation separately from downstream finished-enterprise-SSD manufacturing and delivery constraints.

Rapidly rising server-memory unit values are creating a secondary logistics constraint even though the physical transport network is functioning. Freight forwarders increasingly request shipment splitting and cargo-insurance maximums can limit a single insured shipment to roughly 800–900 64 GB server-memory modules. Physically compact orders therefore require multiple shipments solely because of cargo value, increasing handling, transport complexity, cost and delivery risk. MT·AI labels this effect Logistics Value Constraint.

Current server-memory trading shows that nominal stock materially overstates customer-usable supply. Customer eligibility can depend on country of origin, with non-China production such as Malaysia, Singapore or Taiwan often preferred; original sealed master boxes, sealed inner cartons and sealed trays; and customer- or OEM-specific Micron process/bucket codes. Date codes are currently of low practical importance because circulating stock is generally 2025 or newer. MT·AI defines Effective Available Supply as nominal inventory after these commercial eligibility filters are applied.

Server-memory inventory and outbound shipments are increasingly photographed as transaction evidence. Images are used to verify COO, labels/process codes, batch identity and packaging integrity before shipment, and downstream customers are also requesting photographic confirmation for their own customers. MT·AI treats this as Proof-of-Inventory: visual chain-of-custody evidence has become part of commercial availability in an allocation market, marking a shift from SKU-based to attribute-based and increasingly evidence-based trading.
